When naming organic molecules with multiple functional groups, IUPAC rules dictate a specific priority order for selecting the parent chain:

  1. Principal Functional Group: The chain must contain the highest priority functional group (in this case, the carboxylic acid, $-COOH$), which is assigned position C-1.

  2. Multiple Bonds: The parent chain must include any carbon-carbon double or triple bonds, even if it results in a shorter carbon chain overall.

  • Identify the Principal Functional Group

The molecule contains a carboxylic acid group ($-COOH$). This is the highest priority group, so the suffix of the parent chain will be -oic acid, and its carbon is designated as C-1.

  • Determine the Parent Chain

Starting from C-1, we must trace a path that includes the double bond ($C=C$). Following the path through the double bond gives us a 4-carbon chain ($C_1OOH - C_2 = C_3H - C_4H_3$). Because it contains 4 carbons and a double bond starting at C-2, the base name is but-2-enoic acid (or 2-butenoic acid).

  • Identify and Number Substituents

Looking at our numbered 4-carbon chain, there is a two-carbon ethyl group ($-CH_2CH_3$) attached to carbon-2. This gives us the prefix 2-ethyl.

  • Assemble the Name

Combine the substituent prefix with the parent chain base name to get the full IUPAC name: 2-ethyl-2-butenoic acid.

Final Answer:

The correct option is C (2-Ethyl-2-butenoicacid).

solution:
When naming a secondary amine according to IUPAC rules:

  1. Parent Chain: The longest continuous carbon chain or the largest ring directly attached to the nitrogen atom is selected as the parent chain (giving the root name ending in "-amine").

  2. N-Substituents: The smaller alkyl group attached to the nitrogen is treated as a substituent and is denoted with the locant N-.

  3. Numbering: Numbering of a parent ring always begins at the carbon atom bonded to the amine nitrogen (designated as C-1). The numbering then proceeds around the ring in the direction that assigns the lowest possible locants to any other substituents.

  • Identify the Parent Chain and Functional Group

The nitrogen atom is bonded to an ethyl group (2 carbons) and a substituted cyclopentane ring (5 carbons). Because the ring contains more carbons, it serves as the parent chain. Combined with the amine functional group, the base name is cyclopentanamine.

  • Identify the N-Substituent

The two-carbon group attached directly to the nitrogen is an ethyl group. We designate this as N-ethyl.

  • Number the Parent Ring and Identify Substituents

Assign C-1 to the ring carbon attached to the nitrogen. To give the lowest possible numbers to the remaining substituents, we count around the ring toward the methyl groups. Doing this places the two methyl ($-CH_3$) groups at carbon 3 and carbon 4. Since there are two identical groups, we use the prefix 3,4-dimethyl.

  • Assemble the Name

Combine the N-substituent, the numbered ring substituents, and the parent base name together in alphabetical order (ignoring numerical prefixes like di-).

This gives us: N-ethyl + 3,4-dimethyl + cyclopentanamine.

Final Answer:

The correct IUPAC name is N-ethyl-3,4-dimethylcyclopentanamine, which corresponds to Option B.

question: For which of the following compounds, the IUPAC name is wrong?
solution:
According to IUPAC nomenclature rules for alicyclic compounds, when a principal carbon-containing functional group (such as $-COCl$, $-CONH_2$, $-CN$, or $-COOR$) is bonded directly to a ring, the carbon atom of that functional group is not included in the numbering of the parent ring. To account for this, special suffixes must be used instead of standard open-chain suffixes:

  • $-COCl$: -carbonyl chloride (not -oyl chloride)

  • $-CONH_2$: -carboxamide (not -amide)

  • $-CN$: -carbonitrile (not -nitrile)

  • $-COOR$: -carboxylate (not -oate)

  • Option A (2-methylcyclopentanecarboxamide): The amide group ($-CONH_2$) is directly attached to the cyclopentane ring, so it correctly uses the special suffix "-carboxamide". Numbering the ring starting from this attachment assigns the methyl group to position 2. This name is correct.

  • Option B (Cyclohexanoylchloride): The acid chloride group ($-COCl$) is directly attached to a cyclohexane ring. Therefore, it must use the special suffix "-carbonyl chloride". The provided name incorrectly applies "-oyl chloride", which is strictly reserved for acyclic (open-chain) compounds. The true IUPAC name is cyclohexanecarbonyl chloride. This name is incorrect.

  • Option C (2-Methylcyclobutenecarbonitrile): The nitrile group ($-CN$) is directly attached to the cyclobutene ring, correctly utilizing the special suffix "-carbonitrile". This name is correct.

  • Option D (Methyl-2-bromocyclohexanecarboxylate): The ester group is attached directly to the cyclohexane ring, properly using the special suffix "-carboxylate". The alkyl portion is "methyl", and numbering the ring starting from the ester attachment places the bromo group at position 2. This name is correct.

Final Answer:

The compound with the wrong IUPAC name is Option B.

When naming cyclic compounds with multiple functional groups, IUPAC rules dictate a specific priority order:

  1. Principal Functional Group: The hydroxyl group ($-OH$) has a higher priority than an alkene ($C=C$) or an alkyl substituent ($-CH_3$). The carbon atom attached to the $-OH$ group is always designated as C-1, and the parent name gets the suffix -ol.

  2. Numbering Direction: After assigning C-1, numbering must proceed around the ring in the direction that assigns the lowest possible locant (number) to the next highest priority feature, which is the double bond.

  • Identify the Parent Ring and Principal Group

The molecule is a 4-membered carbon ring (cyclobutane) containing a principal alcohol group ($-OH$). Therefore, the carbon bearing the $-OH$ is C-1, and the base suffix is "-ol".

  • Number the Ring

Starting at C-1, we evaluate both directions around the ring:

  • Path A (Clockwise towards the methyl group): The methyl group is at C-2, and the double bond starts at C-3.

  • Path B (Counter-clockwise towards the double bond): The double bond starts at C-2, and the methyl group is at C-4.

Since the double bond has higher priority than the alkyl substituent for numbering, Path B is the correct numbering scheme because it gives the alkene the lower locant (2 instead of 3).

  • Assemble the Name

  • Substituent: A methyl group at position 4 gives the prefix 4-methyl.

  • Ring & Unsaturation: The 4-carbon ring with a double bond at C-2 is named cyclobut-2-en (or cyclo-2-buten).

  • Suffix: The principal alcohol group at C-1 is -1-ol.

Combining these components gives 4-methylcyclobut-2-en-1-ol (often formatted as 4-Methyl cyclo-2-buten-1-ol).

Final Answer:

The correct IUPAC name is 4-Methyl cyclo-2-buten-1-ol, which corresponds to Option B.

The carbon atom in the ring bonded directly to this $-OH$ group is always designated as position C-1.

  • Determine the parent ring. The core structure is a six-membered saturated carbon ring, which is a cyclohexane. Combining this with the alcohol suffix gives the base name cyclohexanol (or cyclohexan-1-ol).

  • Number the ring and locate substituents. Starting from the alcohol carbon as C-1, we must number the ring in the direction that assigns the lowest possible locants (numbers) to any remaining substituents.

  • Counting in one direction places the two methyl ($-CH_3$) groups at carbon 3.

  • Counting in the other direction would place them at carbon 5.

Since 3 is lower than 5, we use position 3. Because there are two identical methyl groups on that same carbon, we use the prefix 3,3-dimethyl.

  • Assemble the name. Combine the substituent prefix with the parent ring base name.

Putting it all together yields 3,3-dimethylcyclohexanol.

The correct choice is Option C.

D.U. of the compound $=y$

the value of $(x+y)$ is?
question:
Number of carbon present in parent chain of given compound $=x$

D.U. of the compound $=y$

the value of $(x+y)$ is?
solution:
• Parent Carbon Chain (PCC): Following IUPAC nomenclature rules for aldehydes, the longest continuous carbon chain must include the carbonyl carbon of the aldehyde group ($-CHO$), which is always assigned position C-1.

  • Degree of Unsaturation (D.U.): Also known as Double Bond Equivalent (DBE), this represents the total number of rings and pi ($\pi$) bonds present in a molecule.

  • Determine $x$ (Length of the Parent Chain)

Start numbering from the aldehyde carbon as C-1. Tracing the longest continuous path down the zig-zag chain, we reach a junction at C-5. Attached to C-5 is an "Et" (ethyl) group, which contains 2 carbons, and the main backbone which also continues for 2 more carbons. Following the longest continuous path through this junction gives a total maximum chain length of 7 carbon atoms (a heptanal derivative).

Therefore, $x = 7$.

  • Determine $y$ (Degree of Unsaturation)

Observing the structure, it is an open-chain (acyclic) compound, meaning there are 0 rings. The aldehyde functional group ($-CHO$) inherently contains one carbon-oxygen double bond ($C=O$). Because one double bond contains one $\pi$ bond, it contributes 1 to the degree of unsaturation. There are no other double or triple bonds in the molecule.

Therefore, $y = 1$.

  • Calculate the sum ($x + y$)

Substitute the identified values into the final expression:

$x + y = 7 + 1 = 8$

Final Answer:

The correct value is 8.

q: If the given compounds name is $\mathrm{X}, \mathrm{Y}$ dimethylhept-Z-ynenitrile, the value of $X+Y+Z$ is _.
question: If the given compounds name is $\mathrm{X}, \mathrm{Y}$ dimethylhept-Z-ynenitrile, the value of $X+Y+Z$ is _.
solution:
• The principal functional group is the nitrile group ($-\mathrm{C\equiv N}$), which has the highest priority.

  • The carbon of the nitrile group is assigned position 1 ($\mathrm{C\text{-}1}$).

  • The parent chain must include the principal functional group as well as the carbon-carbon triple bond (alkyne).

Tracing the longest continuous carbon chain containing both:

  • $\mathrm{C\text{-}1}$: Nitrile carbon ($-\mathrm{C\equiv N}$)

  • $\mathrm{C\text{-}2}$: Carbon bonded to $\mathrm{C\text{-}1}$, a methyl group ($-\mathrm{CH_3}$), and $\mathrm{C\text{-}3}$

  • $\mathrm{C\text{-}3}$: $-\mathrm{CH_2}-$ carbon

  • $\mathrm{C\text{-}4}$: $-\mathrm{CH_2}-$ carbon

  • $\mathrm{C\text{-}5}$: Carbon bonded to a methyl group ($-\mathrm{CH_3}$) and the alkyne group

  • $\mathrm{C\text{-}6}$: First carbon of the triple bond

  • $\mathrm{C\text{-}7}$: Terminal carbon of the triple bond ($-\mathrm{C\equiv CH}$)

Since the parent chain contains 7 carbon atoms, the root word is hept.

  • Methyl substituents: Located at $\mathrm{C\text{-}2}$ and $\mathrm{C\text{-}5}$, giving 2,5-dimethyl.

  • Triple bond (alkyne): Starts at $\mathrm{C\text{-}6}$, giving hept-6-yne.

  • Principal suffix: Nitrile at $\mathrm{C\text{-}1}$, giving hept-6-ynenitrile.

Combining these gives the IUPAC name:

$$\text{2,5-dimethylhept-6-ynenitrile}$$

Comparing this with the given format, $\mathrm{X, Y\text{-}dimethylhept\text{-}Z\text{-}ynenitrile}$:

  • $X = 2$

  • $Y = 5$

  • $Z = 6$

$$X + Y + Z = 2 + 5 + 6 = 13$$
